results.question: I cast a sorcery with buyback and pay its buyback cost, then copy that spell with [Fork]. Once everything resolves, how many copies of the card end up back in my hand?
results.text:
One copy of the card ends up back in your hand — only the original sorcery card you cast returns; the copy created by Fork does not return a card to your hand.

Reasoning and definitions:
- Buyback is the static ability that “You may pay an additional [cost] as you cast this spell” and “If the buyback cost was paid, put this spell into its owner’s hand instead of into that player’s graveyard as it resolves.” That applies to the actual spell object that was cast from your hand and whose buyback cost you paid [702.27a].
- To copy a spell means to put a copy of it onto the stack; a copy of a spell isn’t cast and thus has no card associated with it [707.10].
- Fork’s rulings make this interaction explicit: Fork’s copy is not considered to have been cast [Fork ruling #9], Fork’s card (Fork) goes to the graveyard when it resolves and there is no card representing the copy on the stack [Fork ruling #10], and if you copy a spell for which Buyback has been paid, you get nothing back from the copy since the copied spell does not have a card to give you [Fork ruling #8].

Putting those points together: because buyback returns the spell card that was actually cast (the original sorcery card) as it resolves, you get that one card back. The copy that Fork put on the stack is not a cast spell and has no card to return, so it doesn’t put anything into your hand [702.27a, 707.10, Fork ruling #8, Fork ruling #9, Fork ruling #10].

results.question: I have a face-down manifested card that's really [Lightning Bolt]. It dies and I imprint it on [Mimic Vat]. Later I activate Mimic Vat's copy ability -- do I get a token?
results.text: No — you don’t get a token. Mimic Vat ruling #0 explicitly says that if the card exiled with Mimic Vat is an instant or sorcery that was manifested (a nonpermanent card), you can have that nonpermanent card exiled but “You can't create a token that's a copy of a nonpermanent card. No token is created in this case.” Lightning Bolt is an Instant, so the card you imprinted with Mimic Vat is a nonpermanent card; activating Mimic Vat’s {3}, {T} ability later will not produce a token copy of Lightning Bolt. You may still activate Mimic Vat’s ability (Mimic Vat ruling #6 says you may activate it even if no card is exiled), but when that ability resolves it won’t create a token for a nonpermanent card exiled with Mimic Vat.

results.question: My [Fiend Hunter]'s enters-the-battlefield ability is on the stack, about to exile a creature. I copy that ability with [Lithoform Engine] and target a second creature. Both get exiled. When Fiend Hunter later leaves the battlefield, do both come back?
results.text:
Yes — both creatures return to the battlefield when Fiend Hunter leaves the battlefield. Fiend Hunter’s enters-the-battlefield ability (which exiles creatures) and Fiend Hunter’s leaves-the-battlefield ability (which returns “the exiled card”) are linked, so the return ability refers only to cards exiled by the enters ability [607.1; 607.2a]. Lithoform Engine’s copy of Fiend Hunter’s enters-the-battlefield ability is also linked to Fiend Hunter’s leaves-the-battlefield ability, so both creatures exiled (the original and the copy) are considered “the exiled card” for the return ability and therefore both return when Fiend Hunter leaves [Lithoform Engine ruling #4; 607.3].

Assumption: the copy resolved and both creatures are currently exiled by those abilities. If Fiend Hunter left the battlefield before its enters-the-battlefield ability resolved, see Fiend Hunter ruling #0 — the leave trigger would resolve first and do nothing, and the subsequently resolving enters ability would exile indefinitely (those exiled creatures would not return). Also note that when those cards return, they are new objects with no relation to their previous existence [Fiend Hunter ruling #1; 400.7].

results.question: My own [Banishing Light] has an opponent's creature exiled. On my opponent's turn I cast [Teferi's Protection], phasing out my Banishing Light. Does the exiled creature return to the battlefield?
results.text:
No. The creature exiled by Banishing Light stays in exile when Banishing Light phases out due to Teferi's Protection; phasing Banishing Light does not cause the exiled creature to return. 

Definition of phasing (key point): Phasing is a status change where a permanent that phases out is treated as though it doesn’t exist and hasn’t changed zones or control; when it phases in its status becomes “phased in” and the game again treats it as though it exists (see rules 702.26d and 702.26c). 

Why the creature stays exiled: Banishing Light’s exile lasts “until this enchantment leaves the battlefield” (Banishing Light). Teferi's Protection ruling #21 explicitly says that “any one-shot effects that are waiting ‘until [this] leaves the battlefield,’ such as that of Banishing Light, won’t happen when a permanent phases out.” In other words, phasing out Banishing Light is not the same as Banishing Light leaving the battlefield, so the “return when Banishing Light leaves the battlefield” event does not occur when Banishing Light phases out (see 702.26d for the rule that phasing doesn’t cause a permanent to change zones). The exiled creature therefore remains in exile until Banishing Light actually leaves the battlefield (or another effect returns the creature). 

Additional note: If the exiled object is a token, Banishing Light ruling #7 says that a token exiled this way will cease to exist and won’t return.

results.question: I cast [Emrakul, the Promised End]. In response to its cast trigger, my opponent tries to [Counterspell] it. Can they even target it given protection from instants, and if it's countered, do I still control their next turn?
results.text:
Yes. Counterspell can target Emrakul, the Promised End while Emrakul, the Promised End is on the stack, and if Counterspell counters Emrakul, the triggered ability created “When you cast Emrakul, the Promised End …” will still resolve so you will still gain control of the target opponent during that player’s next turn (provided that triggered ability’s target is still legal when it resolves). 

Why: Protection is defined as preventing targeting by spells or abilities with the stated quality while the protected object is a permanent on the battlefield (see rule 702.16b and Emrakul, the Promised End ruling #1). Emrakul, the Promised End’s protection from instants applies only while Emrakul, the Promised End is on the battlefield, so Emrakul, the Promised End may be targeted by an instant spell while Emrakul, the Promised End is on the stack (Emrakul, the Promised End ruling #2). Counterspell is an instant that targets a spell on the stack, so it can target Emrakul, the Promised End on the stack. 

When you cast Emrakul, the Promised End that casting event puts its triggered ability (“When you cast this spell, …”) onto the stack (see rule 603.1a). Activated and triggered abilities on the stack aren’t spells and therefore can’t be countered by effects that counter only spells (for example, Counterspell) (see rule 113.9). Because Emrakul, the Promised End’s triggered ability has no intervening “if” clause, it won’t be removed for lack of that clause when it tries to resolve (see rule 608.2a). Therefore, even if Counterspell resolves and counters Emrakul, the Promised End, the triggered ability will still resolve and create the control/delayed extra-turn effect — unless the triggered ability’s target (the opponent) becomes an illegal target by the time the ability resolves, in which case the resolution would fail for that target (see rule 608.2b).

results.question: My cascade spell exiles cards until it hits [Valki, God of Lies], whose back face is the seven-mana planeswalker Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor. Is that a legal cascade hit, and can I cast the Tibalt side for free?
results.text:
Yes. Your cascade can stop on Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor, but you may only cast the Valki, God of Lies face for free; you may not cast the Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor face for free because Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor’s mana value (7) doesn’t meet cascade’s “less than” requirement.

Reasoning and definitions:
- Cascade: As defined by rule 702.85a, when you cast a spell with cascade you exile cards until you exile a nonland card whose mana value is less than that cascading spell’s mana value; you may cast that exiled card without paying its mana cost only if the resulting spell’s mana value is less than the cascading spell’s mana value. (This is the rule determining what cards cascade can “hit” and what you may cast.)
- Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor’s mana value is 2 (from the card’s data). Because that card’s mana value (2) is less than your cascading spell’s mana value, cascade will stop when you exile Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor. You may cast the exiled card only if the resulting spell’s mana value is less than the cascading spell’s mana value (702.85a).
- Casting a modal double-faced card from among a group: The card-specific ruling for Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor allows that “if an effect allows you to play a land or cast a spell from among a group of cards, you may play or cast a modal double-faced card with any face that fits the criteria of that effect” (Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor ruling #16). Applying that here, you may choose which face to cast only if the chosen face’s resulting spell’s mana value satisfies cascade’s “less than” condition.

Application: Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor’s front face (Valki, God of Lies) has mana value 2, so you may cast Valki, God of Lies without paying its mana cost via cascade (assuming the cascade spell’s mana value is greater than 2). Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor’s face would produce a spell with mana value 7, which isn’t less than the cascading spell’s mana value, so you may not cast Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor for free via that cascade.

If you want different timing/edge cases: this answer assumes you’re following cascade’s normal resolution (you finish exiling, then may cast the exiled card). If an effect changed which face’s mana value counts for the card itself, that could change the result, but no such effect is in the situation you described.
citations: Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor
Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor ruling #16

results.question: I cast [Emrakul, the Promised End]. With its cast trigger on the stack, I copy that trigger with [Lithoform Engine]. Then I untap Lithoform Engine with [Voltaic Key] and use it again to copy [Emrakul, the Promised End] itself as a permanent spell. How many of my opponent's turns do I control, do I get a second Emrakul, and does copying the Emrakul spell give me another control-a-turn trigger?
results.text:
You will control your opponent for only one of that opponent’s turns (their next turn), you will get a second Emrakul, the Promised End as a token if the copied permanent spell resolves, and copying the Emrakul, the Promised End spell does not create an additional “When you cast this spell” control-a-turn trigger. 

Reasoning and definitions (so this stands on its own):
- Definition: To “copy” a spell or ability means to put a copy of it onto the stack; a copy of a spell isn’t cast and a copy of an ability isn’t activated (definition of copy and “not cast”) [707.10], [707.10d].
- Definition: A delayed triggered ability is an effect created by another effect or ability that will do something later (it will contain “when,” “whenever,” or “at”) [603.7h]. Emrakul, the Promised End’s resolved cast trigger creates the later effect that makes you gain control of the targeted opponent during that opponent’s next turn and then gives that opponent an extra turn afterward (this is implemented as a delayed/ongoing effect produced when the triggered ability resolves; see Emrakul, the Promised End ruling guidance below).

What happens in your sequence (assuming the copied trigger was put on the stack on top of the original trigger, so the copy resolves first as described):
- Copying the “when you cast this spell” trigger with Lithoform Engine, putting that copy on the stack, produces a second triggered ability on the stack. A copy of a triggered ability is itself an ability and is put on the stack under the controller who created the copy [707.10], [707.10b]. When those two triggered abilities resolve they each create their control/extra-turn effects. Emrakul, the Promised End ruling #14 explains that multiple player-controlling effects that affect the same player overwrite each other and the last one created is the one that actually determines who controls that player’s turn; but each ability will create its extra turn [Emrakul, the Promised End ruling #14]. Therefore you will end up gaining control of that opponent during that opponent’s next turn only once (the last-created control effect overwrites the earlier one) even though two control-producing abilities resolved [Emrakul, the Promised End ruling #14].
- Each resolved trigger also creates an extra turn for that opponent after that next turn; because two triggers resolved, two extra turns are created for that opponent. Extra turns are added one at a time, and the most recently created extra turn is taken first, so the extra-turn ordering will follow creation order (most recently created extra turn happens first) [500.7]. Emrakul, the Promised End ruling #16 explains how skip/extra-turn timing interacts with this effect if turns are skipped [Emrakul, the Promised End ruling #16].
- When you untap Lithoform Engine with Voltaic Key and use Lithoform Engine’s {4}, {T} ability to copy Emrakul, the Promised End as a permanent spell, that copy is created on the stack and is not cast; the copy will become a token as it resolves and then enter the battlefield as that token permanent if it resolves [Lithoform Engine ruling #6], [111.13], [Lithoform Engine ruling #5]. Because the copy wasn’t cast, copying the Emrakul, the Promised End spell does not cause Emrakul, the Promised End’s “When you cast this spell” trigger to be created — creating the copy won’t cause “when you cast” triggers to occur [707.10d], [Lithoform Engine ruling #6]. (You already created a second control trigger earlier by copying the original cast trigger with Lithoform Engine, but the copy-of-the-spell itself does not create another cast trigger.)

Summary of concrete outcomes:
- Number of opponent turns you control: one — you control the targeted opponent during that opponent’s next turn only (the last-created control effect overwrites any earlier one) [Emrakul, the Promised End ruling #14].
- Do you get a second Emrakul, the Promised End? Yes — the copy of the permanent spell created by Lithoform Engine becomes a token as it resolves and will be a second Emrakul, the Promised End permanent if it resolves [111.13], [Lithoform Engine ruling #5], [Lithoform Engine ruling #6].
- Does copying the Emrakul, the Promised End spell give another control-a-turn trigger? No — the copy isn’t cast, and creating the copy won’t cause the “When you cast this spell” trigger to be created; the only way you got a second cast-trigger was by copying the existing triggered ability with Lithoform Engine earlier [707.10], [707.10d], [Lithoform Engine ruling #6].

If you want the precise order of the extra turns: because the copy-of-trigger resolved first and the original trigger resolved second in the assumed timing, the extra turn created when the original trigger resolved (the later-created extra turn) will be taken first, then the extra turn created by the earlier-resolving copy-of-trigger will be taken next [500.7]. If you assumed the triggers resolved in a different order, swap which extra turn is taken first accordingly.

results.question: I've imprinted a creature on [Mimic Vat] and activate its ability to make a token copy. While that ability is on the stack, I copy it with [Lithoform Engine]. Do I get two tokens?
results.text:
Yes — you get two tokens, assuming Mimic Vat has a card exiled by the time each ability resolves. Lithoform Engine’s ability copies the activated ability of Mimic Vat and puts that copy on the stack as a separate instance; the copy’s source is the same Mimic Vat as the original ability, so both the original ability and the copy refer to the same card(s) exiled with Mimic Vat. When each ability resolves, it creates a token that’s a copy of a card exiled with Mimic Vat, so you end up with two tokens. If no card is exiled with Mimic Vat by the time an instance of the ability resolves, that instance creates no token.

Short reasoning and citations: Lithoform Engine’s first ability creates another instance of the activated ability on the stack ([Lithoform Engine ruling #3]) and the copy has the same source as the original ability ([Lithoform Engine ruling #0], [707.10b]). Because the ability’s effect says “Create a token that’s a copy of a card exiled with this artifact,” both instances refer to the cards exiled with Mimic Vat (the same source), and each resolving instance creates its token copy. Mimic Vat’s rulings confirm the token created is a copy of whatever card is exiled with Mimic Vat when the ability resolves and that no token is created if no card is exiled by resolution ([Mimic Vat ruling #4], [Mimic Vat ruling #6]). If multiple cards were exiled with Mimic Vat (for example, due to a melded permanent or multiple exiles), see how such cases are handled ([607.3]).

results.question: An opponent controls an untapped [Trinisphere], and I have a permanent that makes my green spells cost {1} less. I want to cast [Awaken the Woods] for value. If I cast it with X=0, what does it cost and what do I get, and what X should I actually choose?
results.text:
If you announce X=0 for Awaken the Woods you must pay a total of {1}{G}{G} to cast Awaken the Woods and you get 0 tokens. You should instead announce X=2 (announce X as you cast the spell); with your cost-reduction and the opponent’s untapped Trinisphere the total cost you'll pay is still {1}{G}{G}, and choosing X=2 gives you two 1/1 green Forest Dryad land creature tokens for that same total cost.

Why: X is a value the controller of a spell with {X} in its mana cost chooses and announces as part of casting (see rule 107.3a and rule 601.2b). Awaken the Woods’s mana cost is {X}{G}{G} (Awaken the Woods card data). To determine what you actually pay, determine the spell’s mana cost with the chosen X, add any cost increases, apply cost reductions, then apply Trinisphere’s effect if the mana component of the spell’s cost is less than three mana (see rule 601.2f, the Total Cost definition, and [Trinisphere ruling #0]).

Step for X=0: start with {G}{G} (Awaken the Woods with X=0). Apply your green-spell cost reduction (applied in the cost-determination step). After cost reductions the mana component is still less than three, so the opponent’s untapped Trinisphere makes the spell’s total mana requirement up to three mana; the resulting total cost is {1}{G}{G} (per [Trinisphere ruling #0]). You then pay that locked-in total cost and, when Awaken the Woods resolves, you create X = 0 1/1 green Forest Dryad land creature tokens (Awaken the Woods card data).

Why X=2 is best for 'value' here: if you announce X=1, the spell’s initial cost is {1}{G}{G}; after your {1} cost reduction it becomes {G}{G}, and Trinisphere then raises it to {1}{G}{G} — you pay {1}{G}{G} and get one token. If you announce X=2, the spell’s initial cost is {2}{G}{G}; after your {1} cost reduction it becomes {1}{G}{G}, which already totals three so Trinisphere does nothing further — you pay {1}{G}{G} and get two tokens. Announcing X greater than 2 raises the locked-in total cost above {1}{G}{G}, so X=2 maximizes tokens for the same total payment.

Assumptions / timing note: this assumes the opponent’s Trinisphere is untapped and on the battlefield at the moment you determine and lock in the total cost while casting Awaken the Woods (the order of applying cost increases/reductions and then Trinisphere is per [Trinisphere ruling #0] and rule 601.2f). If Trinisphere became tapped or left the battlefield as part of paying a cost, follow [Trinisphere ruling #1] about timing of that change relative to locking in payment.

results.question: [Grist, the Hunger Tide] is in my graveyard. Can I return it with [Animate Dead], and what happens?
results.text:
Yes. You may cast Animate Dead targeting Grist, the Hunger Tide in your graveyard because Grist, the Hunger Tide is a creature card in your graveyard. When Animate Dead resolves, it will try to return that card to the battlefield and attach Animate Dead to it, but Grist, the Hunger Tide becomes a planeswalker (not a creature) as it enters the battlefield. Because Animate Dead’s post‑entry enchantment is only able to enchant a creature put onto the battlefield with that Aura, Animate Dead won’t be able to legally attach to Grist, the Hunger Tide and Animate Dead will be put into your graveyard as a state‑based action; that will cause the Aura’s leave‑the‑battlefield delayed triggered ability to trigger. When that triggered ability resolves, it sacrifices the returned object only “if the creature’s still on the battlefield”; Grist, the Hunger Tide is no longer a creature on the battlefield, so the sacrifice does not apply and Grist, the Hunger Tide remains on the battlefield as a planeswalker. 

Relevant points and where they come from:
- Grist, the Hunger Tide is a creature card while it’s not on the battlefield, so it can be targeted by Animate Dead (Grist, the Hunger Tide ruling #1). 
- Animate Dead’s enter sequence returns the targeted card to the battlefield and attempts to attach the Aura to the new object (Animate Dead ruling #1). 
- If the returned object can’t legally be enchanted by Animate Dead (for example, because it’s not a creature on the battlefield), Animate Dead won’t be able to attach, will be put into the graveyard, and its leave‑the‑battlefield delayed triggered ability will trigger; when that trigger resolves, if the creature is still on the battlefield its controller sacrifices it (Animate Dead ruling #4). 

Assumption about timing: this explanation assumes normal resolution timing of Animate Dead’s enter process and the resulting state‑based action that moves Animate Dead to the graveyard; different explicit timing (for example, if Animate Dead somehow isn’t on the battlefield as its triggered ability resolves) is covered by the cited rulings.

results.question: My commander [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave] has four +1/+1 counters on it. It dies, I move it to the command zone, then recast it. Does it keep the counters, and does [Doubling Season] double them as it re-enters?
results.text:
Yes — Skullbriar, the Walking Grave keeps its four +1/+1 counters when you move Skullbriar, the Walking Grave to the command zone and when you recast Skullbriar, the Walking Grave; Doubling Season does not double those retained counters as Skullbriar, the Walking Grave enters the battlefield.

Why: Skullbriar, the Walking Grave’s printed ability causes counters to remain on Skullbriar, the Walking Grave as it changes zones, so those counters persist when Skullbriar, the Walking Grave goes to the command zone and later when Skullbriar, the Walking Grave returns to the battlefield (see Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #1 and ruling #3 about counters affecting Skullbriar, the Walking Grave in other zones). Normally counters cease to exist when an object changes zones ([122.2], [400.7]), but Skullbriar, the Walking Grave’s text creates the exception.

Why Doubling Season does not double them: Doubling Season doubles counters that are put onto a permanent (including counters put on as that permanent enters the battlefield) (see Doubling Season ruling #2). The counters that “remain” on Skullbriar, the Walking Grave as it changes zones are not considered to have been “placed” or “put on” Skullbriar, the Walking Grave when it re-enters, so Doubling Season does not affect those retained counters (see Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #2). 

Assumption about timing: This answer assumes the sequence you described (Skullbriar, the Walking Grave dies, you move Skullbriar, the Walking Grave to the command zone, then you cast Skullbriar, the Walking Grave). If instead counters were being put onto Skullbriar, the Walking Grave as part of its re-entry effect, Doubling Season could apply to those "put" counters (see Doubling Season ruling #2).

results.question: I cast [Final Fortune] to take an extra turn. During that extra turn I use [Sundial of the Infinite] to end the turn before the end step. Do I still lose the game?
results.text:
No — you do not lose the game.

Definition: To “end the turn” as the result of an effect means to perform an expedited process that skips nearly everything else that would happen that turn (see rule [724.1]).

Reasoning: Final Fortune’s text gives you an extra turn after this one and says “At the beginning of that turn’s end step, you lose the game.” If, during the extra turn from Final Fortune, you activate Sundial of the Infinite to end the turn, Sundial of the Infinite’s ability is an effect that ends the turn ([Sundial of the Infinite ruling #4]; see rule [724.1d]). Ending the turn this way skips the end step, so anything that would happen “at the beginning of the end step” doesn’t get to happen that turn ([Sundial of the Infinite ruling #1]; see rule [724.1e]). Final Fortune’s specific punishment (“At the beginning of that turn’s end step, you lose the game.”) therefore never occurs on the turn you ended early. Moreover, the rules for Final Fortune explicitly cover this interaction: “If you end up skipping the extra turn that is gained, you do not lose the game.” ([Final Fortune ruling #1]; Final Fortune card text).

Conclusion: Because Sundial of the Infinite’s end-the-turn effect causes the end step to be skipped, the “At the beginning of that turn’s end step, you lose the game.” instruction from Final Fortune does not occur, and you do not lose the game.

If you want a quick ruling reference: this follows from [724.1], [724.1d], [724.1e], [Sundial of the Infinite ruling #4], [Sundial of the Infinite ruling #1], and [Final Fortune ruling #1].

results.question: I cast [Clone]. When and how do I choose what it copies, and can my opponent respond to that choice?
results.text:
Direct answer: You choose what Clone copies as Clone is entering the battlefield — not when you cast Clone. That choice is made by Clone’s controller as part of applying replacement effects to the event “Clone enters the battlefield.” Because the choice is part of the entering-the-battlefield replacement process (not a spell or ability on the stack), opponents don’t get priority to respond to that choice itself; they can only respond before Clone’s spell resolves or after Clone has entered the battlefield.

Reasoning and details:
- Clone’s printed ability lets you have Clone “enter as a copy of any creature on the battlefield,” so the decision is an “as this enters” choice related to the entering-the-battlefield event (see Clone ruling #0 and Clone ruling #5). The controller of Clone makes any such “as this enters” choices for Clone (see rule 707.6).
- An object that enters the battlefield “as a copy” becomes a copy as it enters the battlefield; that is, the copying and any “as . . . enters” effects are applied while the object is entering (rule 707.5). Clone can only copy a creature that is already on the battlefield (Clone ruling #2).
- If replacement effects (including ones that would make the entering object a copy) are available to modify the same event, the affected object’s controller chooses which to apply at that time (rules 616.1c and 616.1d). That choice is part of resolving the event, not a spell or ability being put on the stack.
- Because the choice happens as part of applying replacement effects to the enter-the-battlefield event, it is not an action that goes on the stack; players do not receive priority between making that choice and the object entering. Players can, however, respond while Clone is still a spell on the stack (before it resolves) or after Clone finishes entering the battlefield.

Timing note (assumption): The answer assumes the normal timing where you cast Clone, Clone’s spell resolves, and then Clone would enter the battlefield. If Clone would somehow be entering simultaneously with another creature, you cannot choose that simultaneously entering creature as the copy (Clone ruling #2).

results.question: I activate my [Flooded Strand]'s ability, then activate [Gogo, Master of Mimicry] with X=2 to copy it twice. How many lands do I get from that one Flooded Strand?
results.text:
You get three lands total: one from the original Flooded Strand activation plus two more from the two copies created by Gogo, Master of Mimicry.

Reasoning and definitions (assumption: you activated Flooded Strand’s ability and paid its activation costs, so Flooded Strand was tapped and sacrificed as part of that activation before Gogo, Master of Mimicry was activated):
- To “copy” an activated ability means to put a copy of that ability onto the stack; a copy of an activated ability isn’t activated and copies the characteristics and decisions of the original, but not choices made on resolution (definition and effects of copies). [707.10b]
- When you activated Flooded Strand’s ability you put that activated ability on the stack; when you then activated Gogo, Master of Mimicry with X=2 targeting that Flooded Strand ability, Gogo, Master of Mimicry’s ability created two additional instances (copies) of the Flooded Strand activated ability on the stack. [Gogo, Master of Mimicry ruling #6]
- Each copy is put on the stack as an ability whose source is the same as the original Flooded Strand ability, and if the copy’s effect refers to objects used to pay the original ability’s costs it uses those objects used to pay the original costs. That means the copies do not require paying Flooded Strand’s costs again; they operate using the fact you already paid those costs. [707.10b; Gogo, Master of Mimicry ruling #9]
- Because the original Flooded Strand activated ability plus the two copies are three separate instances on the stack, each can (and will) resolve separately. Each resolution lets you search your library for a Plains or Island and put it onto the battlefield (choices made on resolution are made separately for each instance). [707.10b; Flooded Strand]

Therefore you will put three lands onto the battlefield in total (one per resolving instance: the original Flooded Strand ability and the two copies from Gogo, Master of Mimicry).
